explanation: 1 Chronicles 18:2 records that David defeated Moab, and 'the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.' Option B, 'completely annihilated with no one left' (wrong_detail), is incorrect because the text says they became servants and paid tribute, meaning they continued to exist. Option C, 'a peace covenant was made and they became allies' (common_misconception), is the opposite of the vassal relationship the text describes. Option D, 'sent hostages to David as a guarantee' (wrong_detail), adds a detail not present in this verse; what the text states is the payment of tribute.

content: When King Tou of Hamath sent his son to congratulate David for defeating Hadadezer, how did David handle the articles of gold, silver, and bronze he received?
options: He dedicated them to the LORD along with the spoils taken from other nations
He stored them in the royal treasury for future use when needed
He distributed them all to the soldiers who had fought in those battles
He returned them all to King Tou as a sign of establishing an alliance
explanation: 1 Chronicles 18:11 records that King David 'dedicated these to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he had carried off from all the nations, from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and Amalek.' One must read verse 11 carefully to distinguish this, since verses 9–10 only describe King Tou sending his son Hadoram with gold, silver, and bronze. Option B, 'stored in the royal treasury' (common_misconception), contradicts David's act of dedicating them to the LORD. Option C, 'distributed to the soldiers' (wrong_detail), is close in spirit to sharing spoils but incorrect given the act of dedication described in the text. Option D, 'returned to King Tou' (wrong_detail), confuses the giver of the gifts with how David used them; verse 11 clearly states he dedicated them to the LORD.

content: In the list of David's court officials at the end of chapter 18, who was placed in charge of the Cherethites and Pelethites, and what does the relationship between this position and the others reveal?
options: Benaiah son of Jehoiada commanded the personal guard, a separate unit from the main army led by Joab
Joab son of Zeruiah commanded both the main army and oversaw the Cherethite guard
Abiathar son of Ahimelech served both as priest and as commander of the personal guard
Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud served both as recorder and as commander of the Cherethites
explanation: 1 Chronicles 18:15–17 lists: 'Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army… Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites.' Comparing the list shows that the commander of the personal guard (Benaiah) was distinct from the commander-in-chief of the army (Joab), reflecting a division of military authority. Option B (near_passage) assigns both positions to Joab, but the text states Joab commanded only the main army. Option C (wrong_detail) is incorrect because Abiathar was a priest (verse 16), not the commander of the guard. Option D (wrong_detail) is incorrect because Jehoshaphat was the recorder (verse 15), not the commander of the Cherethites. Cross-referencing each line of the list is required to select the correct answer.

content: According to 1 Chronicles 19:1-2, why did David send messengers to comfort Hanun?
options: Because Nahash, Hanun's father, had just died
Because the Ammonites had just suffered a great defeat
Because Hanun had just ascended the throne and requested a treaty
Because the land of Ammon had just been struck by famine
explanation: 1 Chronicles 19:1-2 records: 'After this Nahash the king of the Ammonites died, and his son reigned in his place. And David said, "I will deal kindly with Hanun the son of Nahash, for his father dealt kindly with me."' So the reason was the death of Nahash, Hanun's father. 'The Ammonites had just suffered a great defeat' is incorrect — the battle occurred AFTER this point (wrong_detail). 'Hanun had just ascended the throne and requested a treaty' confuses David's initiative in showing kindness with Hanun seeking peace (wrong_detail). 'A famine ravaging the land' does not appear in the text at all — it is a fabricated detail (wrong_scope).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 19:4, how did Hanun humiliate David's messengers?
options: He imprisoned them and demanded a large ransom
He shaved them and cut their garments in half
He gouged out the right eye of each of them
He bound them and paraded them throughout Rabbah
explanation: 1 Chronicles 19:4 records: 'So Hanun took David's servants and shaved them and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away.' The correct answer is shaving their beards and cutting their garments. 'Gouging out the right eye' refers to Nahash's threat against the people of Jabesh-gilead in 1 Samuel 11, not here (near_passage). 'Imprisoning them and demanding ransom' and 'binding and parading them throughout the city' are fabricated actions not found in the text (wrong_detail).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 19:10-11, when Joab saw that the battle line was set against him both in front and in the rear, whom did he put in command of part of the troops?
options: Abishai, his brother
Asahel, a mighty warrior
Shobach, the commander of the army
King David himself
explanation: 1 Chronicles 19:11 records: 'The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and they were arrayed against the Ammonites.' So Joab put Abishai in command of those troops. 'Asahel' was another brother in the same family as Joab but is not mentioned in this particular battle (near_passage). 'Shobach' was the commander of the Aramean army — he was on the enemy side and could not have been given command by Joab (wrong_scope). 'David himself' is wrong because the king did not go out to battle in this passage (wrong_detail).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 20:1, where was David while Joab led the army to besiege and destroy Rabbah?
options: Leading the vanguard of the army
Hiding in the wilderness of Judah
Remaining in Jerusalem
Encamped beside the Jordan River
explanation: 1 Chronicles 20:1 records: 'Joab... came and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem.' The correct answer is that David remained in Jerusalem. 'Leading the vanguard' directly contradicts the text (wrong_detail). 'Hiding in the wilderness of Judah' belongs to the period when David was fleeing from Saul, long before this event (wrong_scope). 'Encamped beside the Jordan River' is a fabricated detail not found in this passage (wrong_detail).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 19:6-7, what did the Ammonites do to prepare to face David after they realized they had made themselves odious to him?
options: They abandoned their chariots to surrender and seek peace with David
They paid a thousand talents of silver to hire Aramean chariots and horsemen
They mustered all the Ammonites and asked Moab for reinforcements
They withdrew entirely into Rabbah and fortified it while awaiting a siege
explanation: 1 Chronicles 19:6-7 records that the Ammonites 'sent a thousand talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen' from Aram, and hired thirty-two thousand chariots along with the king of Maacah and his army. So the correct answer refers to using silver to hire Aramean chariots and cavalry. 'Surrendering and seeking peace' is the complete opposite of their hostile posture (wrong_detail). 'Asking Moab for reinforcements' substitutes the wrong nation — the text names Aram, not Moab (wrong_detail). 'Withdrawing into Rabbah to fortify it' is the development that occurs in chapter 20 later on, not the preparation described here (near_passage).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 19:16–18, why did the Arameans, after being defeated by Israel the first time, return to fight again?
options: Because they sent messengers to bring more Arameans from beyond the river
Because Hanun promised to pay double the silver they had previously been hired for
Because King Maacah personally led his full force to take revenge
Because they allied with the Philistines to besiege David together
explanation: 1 Chronicles 19:16 records: 'When the Arameans saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they sent messengers to bring out the Arameans who were beyond the river… and Shophach… went before them.' So they reinforced with Arameans from beyond the Euphrates. 'Hanun promising double payment' is a fabricated motive — the text says nothing about money this time (wrong_detail). 'Maacah personally leading to take revenge' is mistaken — Maacah appears during the initial hiring (v.7), whereas this second engagement involves the army from beyond the river led by Shophach (near_passage). 'Alliance with the Philistines' confuses this passage with other battles; it is not found here (wrong_scope).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 20:2, when Rabbah was captured, what made the crown taken from the head of the king of the Ammonites particularly noteworthy?
options: It was inlaid with an image of Milcom, the god of the Ammonites
It weighed a talent of gold and had precious stones set in it
It had previously belonged to Nahash, their former king
It was placed on David's head right there on the battlefield
explanation: 1 Chronicles 20:2 records that David took the crown of their king, and 'he found that it weighed a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone; and it was placed on David's head.' The notable feature is therefore its weight of a talent of gold together with the precious stones. 'Inlaid with the image of Milcom' is an incorrect detail — Milcom is the god of the Ammonites, but the text makes no mention of his image on the crown (wrong_detail). 'Had previously belonged to Nahash' is an inference beyond what the text states (wrong_scope). 'Placed on David's head right on the battlefield' is partly correct regarding the crowning, but the question targets the crown's distinguishing characteristics, and the text does not specify 'right on the battlefield' (true_but_off).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 20:6–7, what physical characteristic did the giant have who was killed by Jonathan, the son of Shimea, David's brother?
options: He was six cubits tall and wore armor weighing five thousand shekels
He had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot
His spear shaft was like a weaver's beam
He was the brother of Goliath, the man of Gath
explanation: 1 Chronicles 20:6 records that this man of Gath 'had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number; and he also was descended from the giants.' The correct characteristic is therefore six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot. 'Six cubits tall, armor of five thousand shekels' describes Goliath in 1 Samuel 17, not this man (near_passage). 'Spear shaft like a weaver's beam' belongs to Lahmi, the brother of Goliath, in the immediately preceding verse 5 (near_passage). 'Brother of Goliath' also refers to Lahmi in verse 5, not the six-fingered man (near_passage).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 21:3–6, how are Joab's attitude and actions toward David's order to take a census of the people described?
options: He objected but still counted all of Israel and Judah
He objected but obeyed, yet did not count the tribe of Levi or Benjamin
He agreed and eagerly went throughout the land to count the people for the king
He refused outright, so David had to send someone else in his place
explanation: 1 Chronicles 21:3 records that Joab remonstrated: 'Why should my lord require this? Why should it be a cause of guilt for Israel?' But because the king's command prevailed over him, he went and counted the people (v.4). Verse 6 states clearly: 'But he did not include Levi and Benjamin in the numbering, for the king's command was abhorrent to Joab.' So he objected but obeyed, yet omitted Levi and Benjamin — a correct answer that requires holding together both his attitude (v.3) and the exception (v.6). 'Counted all of both tribes' overlooks the exception stated in verse 6 (wrong_detail). 'Agreed and eagerly went' contradicts his explicit remonstrance (wrong_detail). 'Refused outright, king sent someone else' is wrong because Joab himself carried out the census and reported the figures to the king in verse 5 (wrong_detail).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 21:26–28, what sign showed that God had accepted the offering David made at the threshing floor, leading the king to continue offering sacrifices there?
options: A cloud of glory covered the newly built altar
Fire came down from heaven and consumed the offering on the altar
The angel sheathed his sword and the plague immediately ceased
The prophet Gad announced that the plague had stopped
explanation: 1 Chronicles 21:26 records: 'David… called upon the LORD, and He answered him with fire from heaven upon the altar of burnt offering.' It was this very sign of fire from heaven that caused the king to know his offering was accepted and to continue offering sacrifices at that place (v.28). 'A cloud of glory' confuses this event with the dedication of the tabernacle or temple — it is not the sign given here (common_misconception). 'The angel sheathing his sword' is the angel's subsequent action recorded in verse 27, not the sign of God accepting the offering that the question is asking about (true_but_off). 'Gad announcing the plague had ceased' misidentifies the prophet Gad's role — Gad conveyed the command to build the altar (v.18) but did not announce the sign of divine acceptance (wrong_detail).

content: When preparing materials to build the temple, David ordered a certain group living in the land of Israel to be gathered for the task of stone cutting. Which group was this?
options: Foreigners residing in the land
Priests of the line of Aaron
Skilled warriors
Young Levites
explanation: According to 1 Chronicles 22:2, David commanded that the foreigners living in the land of Israel be gathered, and he set stonecutters to prepare stones for building the house of God. The priests of Aaron's line served in sacrifice, not in stone cutting (wrong_scope). Warriors belonged to the military sphere, not to this construction work (wrong_scope). The Levites were assigned to serve in the temple later (ch. 23), not as the initial group of stone cutters (near_passage).

content: David explained why he himself had to prepare materials in advance for the project, even though his son would be the actual builder. What reason did he give?
options: Solomon was young and inexperienced
Solomon was occupied with warfare
Solomon had not yet been anointed
Solomon was far from the capital
explanation: According to 1 Chronicles 22:5, David said, 'Solomon my son is young and inexperienced,' so he prepared abundantly in advance for the magnificent temple. Solomon was not occupied with warfare — it was precisely the coming peace that was the reason his son would build it (wrong_detail). The anointing was not the reason David stated here (wrong_scope). No geographical distance was mentioned at all (wrong_detail).

content: In his words of encouragement to Solomon, David tied his son's success to a condition. What was the core condition he emphasized?
options: Carefully observing the statutes and ordinances the LORD commanded through Moses
Forming alliances with neighboring kings for security
Accumulating much gold and silver for the project
Expanding the borders before beginning construction
explanation: According to 1 Chronicles 22:13, David told Solomon that he would prosper if he carefully observed the statutes and ordinances that the LORD had commanded Moses for Israel; he then added, 'Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid.' Political alliances are not the condition stated — peace comes from the LORD (wrong_scope). Accumulating gold and silver was what David had already done, not a condition for Solomon's success (true_but_off). Expanding the borders was not part of this charge (wrong_detail).

content: In describing the quantity of materials he had prepared, what did David say about certain materials to convey an immense scale beyond measure?
options: Iron and bronze were so abundant they could not be weighed
All the materials came from the spoils of surrounding nations
The gold was taken entirely from the royal treasury
The silver was twice the amount of gold prepared
explanation: According to 1 Chronicles 22:14, David stated he had prepared 100,000 talents of gold and 1,000,000 talents of silver, and that 'bronze and iron beyond weighing, for there is so much of it.' The text does not say everything came from the spoils of surrounding nations (wrong_detail). It does not say the gold was taken entirely from the royal treasury (wrong_scope). The claim that the silver was double the gold is fabricated and does not match the stated figures of 100,000 talents of gold and 1,000,000 talents of silver (wrong_detail).

content: David called on Israel's leaders to help Solomon, reminding them of a present reality as the foundation for his appeal. What was that reality?
options: God had granted them rest on every side
Enemy nations still surrounded them
The Ark of the Covenant was still in a tent
The people were suffering famine due to drought
explanation: According to 1 Chronicles 22:18, David said, 'Is not the LORD your God with you? And has he not given you rest on every side?' The idea that 'enemy nations still surrounded them' contradicts the very rest just proclaimed (wrong_detail). The Ark of the Covenant is mentioned in verse 19 as something to be brought into the temple, not as the foundational reality in verse 18 (near_passage). Famine due to drought is not mentioned at all (wrong_scope).

content: When David numbered the Levites for their service assignments, from what age did he count in the first census recorded?
options: From thirty years old and upward
From twenty years old and upward
From twenty-five years old and upward
From fifty years old and upward
explanation: According to 1 Chronicles 23:3, the Levites were numbered "from thirty years old and upward," totaling 38,000. The age of twenty was a later adjustment within the same chapter (vv. 24, 27), not the figure in verse 3 (near_passage). Twenty-five was the threshold in Numbers 8:24, a different context (wrong_scope). Fifty was the retirement age from heavy service according to Numbers, not the starting age here (common_misconception).

content: David divided the Levites into divisions according to the lineage of the sons of Levi. What were the three original groups by which he organized them?
options: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari
Aaron, Moses, and Miriam
Reuben, Simeon, and Levi
Eleazar, Ithamar, and Phinehas
explanation: According to 1 Chronicles 23:6, David organized the Levites according to the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Aaron and Moses were descendants of Kohath, not the three original groups; Miriam did not establish a division (wrong_scope). Reuben and Simeon were other tribes, not of the Levitical line (wrong_detail). Eleazar and Ithamar were sons of Aaron, used to divide the priestly divisions in chapter 24, not the basis for organizing the Levites (near_passage).

content: After the ark of the covenant had found a resting place and the temple was about to be built, David redefined the role of the Levites differently from before. What was the core change in their duties?
options: They no longer carried the tabernacle but were assigned to assist the descendants of Aaron in serving the temple
They were elevated to replace the priests in offering burnt offerings on the altar
They were given authority to sit in judgment over all disputes of the people in the cities
They had to continue carrying the ark of the covenant throughout the land as they had always done before
explanation: According to 1 Chronicles 23:26–32, because the ark had a resting place, the Levites "need not carry the tabernacle," and their duties shifted to assisting the descendants of Aaron in serving the house of the LORD: caring for the courts, the chambers, the purification of all holy things, the showbread, the fine flour, and keeping watch. They did not replace the priests in offering burnt offerings — that was the exclusive duty of the line of Aaron (common_misconception). The authority to judge in the cities is mentioned elsewhere (ch. 26:29), not the core change here (wrong_scope). Continuing to carry the ark throughout the land is the opposite of the reason "no longer need to carry" (wrong_detail).

content: When dividing the priestly divisions from the two branches of Eleazar and Ithamar, what method did David use to determine the order, so as to avoid partiality between the two branches?
options: Casting lots before the leaders and the priests
Arranging the order by age from oldest to youngest
Letting the king appoint each division at his own discretion
Allowing the two branches to negotiate the division among themselves
explanation: According to 1 Chronicles 24:5, the divisions were assigned "by lot," without distinction between branches, since both had officers of the sanctuary and officers of God. Arranging by age contradicts the impartial nature of casting lots (wrong_detail). The king appointing them himself conflicts with the spirit of impartiality that casting lots was meant to ensure (common_misconception). The two branches negotiating among themselves is not the method described (wrong_scope).

content: In the list of priestly divisions determined by lot, which division drew the first lot — a detail later connected to the genealogy of Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, in the New Testament?
options: Jehoiarib
Abijah
Jedaiah
Harim
explanation: According to 1 Chronicles 24:7, the first lot fell to Jehoiarib, and the second to Jedaiah. Abijah was the eighth division (v. 10) — this is actually the division of Zechariah in Luke 1:5, so it is easily confused with "the first division" (common_misconception). Jedaiah drew the second lot, not the first (near_passage). Harim drew the third lot (v. 8), not the top of the list (wrong_detail). One must distinguish the order of the lots from the New Testament-connected division to answer correctly.

content: According to 1 Chronicles 25, which three men's descendants did David and the army commanders set apart to prophesy through song in the service of the house of the LORD?
options: Korah, Heman, and Jeduthun
Asaph, Heman, and Samuel
Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun
Asaph, Obed-Edom, and Jeduthun
explanation: 1 Chronicles 25:1 records that David and the army commanders set apart the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun to prophesy with lyres, harps, and cymbals. (1) 'Korah, Heman, and Jeduthun' replaces Asaph with Korah — the Korahites belonged to the gatekeeping division in chapter 26, not the singers (near_passage). (2) 'Asaph, Heman, and Samuel' replaces Jeduthun with Samuel — Samuel was an ancestor of Heman, not the leader of a singing division (wrong_detail). (3) 'Asaph, Obed-Edom, and Jeduthun' inserts Obed-Edom — he was the blessed gatekeeper described in chapter 26 (wrong_scope).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 25, what instruments were the singers' sons set apart to use for prophesying?
options: Trumpets, harps, and tambourines
Lyres, harps, and cymbals
Lyres, trumpets, and cymbals
Harps, flutes, and cymbals
explanation: 1 Chronicles 25:1 states they prophesied with lyres, harps, and cymbals. (1) 'Trumpets, harps, and tambourines' introduces trumpets and tambourines — these are not listed among the instruments of this singing division (wrong_detail). (2) 'Lyres, trumpets, and cymbals' replaces harps with trumpets — trumpets were blown by the priests, not the singers (wrong_detail). (3) 'Harps, flutes, and cymbals' omits lyres and adds flutes — this does not match the text (wrong_detail).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 26, which gatekeeper is described as having many sons because God blessed him?
options: Meshelemiah
Hosah
Korah
Obed-Edom
explanation: 1 Chronicles 26:4–5 lists the sons of Obed-Edom and explicitly states 'for God blessed Obed-Edom.' (1) 'Meshelemiah' was also the leader of a gatekeeping division with sons (26:1–2), but the text does not attach the blessing language to him (near_passage). (2) 'Hosah' was another gatekeeper (26:10) but is not accompanied by the blessing statement (near_passage). (3) 'Korah' was the ancestral founder of the gatekeeping line, not the individual described as blessed here (wrong_scope).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 27, how many men were in each division that served the king on a rotating basis, and for how long did each division serve?
options: 12,000 men, one division per month
24,000 men, one division per month
24,000 men, one division per week
30,000 men, one division per month
explanation: 1 Chronicles 27:1 states that each division consisted of 24,000 men, taking turns serving one month at a time throughout the year. (1) '12,000 men, one division per month' changes the troop count to 12,000 — this contradicts the text (wrong_detail). (2) '24,000 men, one division per week' has the correct number but changes the rotation cycle to weekly — the text specifies monthly service (wrong_detail). (3) '30,000 men, one division per month' changes the troop count to 30,000 (wrong_detail).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 25, what principle of assignment does the casting of lots for the singers' duty rotations reflect?
options: Only the elders and teachers were permitted to cast lots
Those who sang better received earlier duty rotations
Young and old, teacher and student alike, all cast lots equally
The firstborn of each household received priority over younger sons
explanation: 1 Chronicles 25:8 records that they cast lots for their assignments, 'small and great alike, teacher as well as student' — indicating fairness regardless of age or status. (1) 'Only the elders and teachers were permitted to cast lots' reverses the very point of the verse, excluding the young and students whom the text explicitly includes (wrong_detail, almost-right for retaining half the list correctly). (2) 'Those who sang better received earlier duty rotations' introduces a skill-based criterion — the text uses lots, not talent rankings (common_misconception). (3) 'The firstborn of each household received priority over younger sons' applies the principle of birthright — that is not the principle operative here (true_but_off).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 25, by what title was Heman called, and what special gift did God give him?
options: Prophet of the king, given twelve sons and two daughters
Seer of the king, given fourteen sons and three daughters
Seer of the king, given seven sons and seven daughters
Priest of the king, given fourteen sons and three daughters
explanation: 1 Chronicles 25:5 calls Heman 'the king's seer' and states that God gave him fourteen sons and three daughters. (1) 'Prophet of the king, twelve sons and two daughters' uses a near-synonym for 'seer' but changes the number of children — wrong on an important detail (wrong_detail, almost-right). (2) 'Seer of the king, seven sons and seven daughters' keeps the correct title but changes the count to 7 and 7 (wrong_detail). (3) 'Priest of the king' changes the title to priest — Heman belonged to the Levitical singers, not the priesthood (wrong_scope).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 26, when lots were cast to assign gates to the gatekeepers, which gate fell to the descendants of Obed-edom and which fell to Hosah?
options: Obed-edom received the east gate, Hosah received the north gate
Obed-edom received the west gate, Hosah received the south gate
Obed-edom received the south gate, Hosah received the west gate
Obed-edom received the north gate, Hosah received the west gate
explanation: 1 Chronicles 26:15–16 records that the lot for the south fell to Obed-edom, while Shuppim and Hosah received the west. (1) 'Obed-edom east, Hosah north' — the east gate fell to Shelemiah (Meshelemiah) and the north to Zechariah, not these two (near_passage, almost-right since the names are correct but the directions are wrong). (2) 'Obed-edom west, Hosah south' — reverses the correct directions of the two men (wrong_detail, almost-right). (3) 'Obed-edom north, Hosah west' — assigns north to Obed-edom when he received the south (wrong_detail).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 27, among David's counselors, who is specifically named as 'the king's friend'?
options: Ahithophel, the king's counselor
Jonathan, the king's uncle
Hushai the Archite
Jehoiada, son of Benaiah
explanation: 1 Chronicles 27:33 records that Ahithophel was the king's counselor, while Hushai the Archite was 'the king's friend.' (1) 'Ahithophel, the king's counselor' is correctly identified as counselor but does not bear the title 'the king's friend' — this is the closest trap (wrong_detail, almost-right). (2) 'Jonathan, the king's uncle' is described as a wise counselor and scribe (27:32) but is not called the king's friend (near_passage). (3) 'Jehoiada, son of Benaiah' was also a counselor succeeding Ahithophel (27:34) but does not bear this title (near_passage).

content: According to 1 Chronicles 27, why was the census that Joab began never fully recorded in the chronicles of King David, and whom had David chosen not to count?
options: Joab completed the count but the king concealed the register in the treasury; David did not count those over sixty years old
Wrath fell on Israel because of the census, so it was not fully recorded; David did not count those twenty years old and under
Wrath fell because of the census, so it was not fully recorded; David did not count the tribes of Levi and Benjamin
Joab refused to complete the census; David did not count those twenty years old and under or the Levites
explanation: 1 Chronicles 27:23–24 states that David did not number those who were twenty years old or under; Joab began the counting but did not finish, and wrath fell on Israel, so the number was not entered in the chronicles of King David. (1) 'Joab completed the count... did not count those over sixty' is wrong on both counts: Joab did NOT finish, and the threshold was twenty and under, not over sixty (wrong_detail). (2) 'Did not count Levi and Benjamin' is correct about the wrath but the exclusion of Levi and Benjamin is a detail from the census in chapter 21, not the reason stated in 27:24 (near_passage, almost-right since it correctly references a real event but from the wrong passage). (3) 'Joab refused to complete... and did not count the Levites' blends Joab's objection in chapter 21 with the age criterion — combining details from different passages (wrong_scope, almost-right). One must cross-reference chapter 21 to distinguish them.

content: According to 1 Chronicles 26, the dedicated treasuries of the house of God held sacred things consecrated by whom, and what did those donors have in common?
options: Moses, Joshua, Saul and Joab — all were commanders who gave a tenth of the spoils of war
Samuel, David, Abner and Joab — all were kings and commanders who gave gold from the tabernacle
Samuel, Saul, Nathan and Joab — all were prophets and commanders who gave burnt offerings
Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab — all were leaders who dedicated things from the spoils of war
explanation: 1 Chronicles 26:27–28 records that the dedicated treasuries held things consecrated by Samuel, Saul son of Kish, Abner son of Ner, and Joab son of Zeruiah — taken from the spoils of war to maintain the house of the LORD. (1) 'Moses, Joshua, Saul and Joab' replaces the first two names with Moses and Joshua — they belong to an earlier era and do not appear in this list (wrong_detail). (2) 'Samuel, David, Abner and Joab' substitutes Saul with David — David was the one who established the storehouses but is not among the four who consecrated things in this verse (near_passage, almost-right since three names are correct). (3) 'Samuel, Saul, Nathan and Joab' replaces Abner with Nathan and changes the dedicated items to burnt offerings — wrong on both the person and the type of offering (wrong_detail, almost-right). One must remember exactly the four names and the source as 'spoils of war' to eliminate the distractors.

content: As David was nearing death, to what place did he summon all the leaders of Israel to deliver his final charge?
options: Jerusalem
Hebron
Bethlehem
Shiloh
explanation: 1 Chronicles 28:1 states that David assembled all the officials of Israel in Jerusalem. Hebron was where David reigned for his first seven years, but it was not the site of this assembly (wrong_detail). Bethlehem was David's hometown, not the location of this event (true_but_off). Shiloh had once served as the site of the tabernacle in earlier times but has no connection to this occasion (wrong_scope).

content: What reason did David give for why God did not permit him to build the temple, relating to his own life?
options: Because he was a man of war and had shed blood
Because he was old and had grown weak
Because he was not of the Levitical priestly line
Because he had worshiped idols in his youth
explanation: 1 Chronicles 28:3 records that God told David he could not build the temple because he was a warrior who had shed blood. David's age is mentioned elsewhere but is not the stated reason he was forbidden to build (wrong_detail). Not belonging to the Levitical line is not the reason given in the text (common_misconception). David never worshiped idols — this detail is an invention with no basis in the text (wrong_detail).
tags: Reason for not building the temple

content: David gave Solomon the plans for the temple. According to the text, where did David say these plans came from?
options: By the Spirit's revelation and written by the hand of the LORD so that David understood it clearly
By Solomon's own hand, having drawn everything out himself beforehand
By skilled craftsmen from Tyre in the north, who designed them and sent them
By the prophet Nathan, who saw them in a night vision and relayed them to the king
explanation: 1 Chronicles 28:12 and 28:19 state that David received the plans by the Spirit's prompting, and that 'all this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD' so that he understood it. Solomon received the plans; he did not draw them himself (wrong_detail). The craftsmen of Tyre later supplied materials and labor, but the plans themselves came from the LORD (true_but_off). Nathan was David's prophet, but the text does not attribute the plans to him (near_passage).

content: David warned Solomon about the consequence of forsaking God. What did he say would happen?
options: God will reject him forever
God will delay the building of the temple
God will remove the throne from his lineage temporarily
God will bring disaster upon the whole nation
explanation: 1 Chronicles 28:9 records: 'if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever.' Delaying the temple construction is not the consequence stated in this verse (near_passage). Removing the throne 'temporarily' sounds plausible but the text says 'cast off forever,' not temporarily (wrong_detail). Bringing disaster upon the whole nation is a consequence from a different episode — such as the census — not from this warning to Solomon (wrong_scope).

content: Beyond what he had already prepared for the temple, David donated Ophir gold from his own private treasury. Why did he emphasize that this was his personal wealth?
options: Because of his love for the house of God, he gave even his own personal wealth
Because the common treasury was depleted and he felt compelled to make up the difference
Because the law required the king to contribute a tenth of his personal wealth
Because he expected the officials to repay him the full amount afterward
explanation: 1 Chronicles 29:3 records David saying: 'Moreover, in addition to all that I have provided for the holy house, I have a treasure of my own of gold and silver, and because of my devotion to the house of my God I give it to the house of my God.' The text says nothing about the common treasury being depleted (wrong_detail). No tithe law governing this situation is mentioned here (common_misconception). David gave freely and generously, with no expectation of repayment (wrong_detail).

content: When the people and their leaders willingly gave generously for the building of the temple, what was their reaction and that of King David?
options: They rejoiced because they had given wholeheartedly, and King David also rejoiced greatly
They were sad at heart because they had given away so much of their wealth and possessions
They began to argue with one another about who had given more than the others
They united in asking the king to exempt them from taxes for the entire coming year
explanation: 1 Chronicles 29:9 records that the people rejoiced because they had given willingly to the LORD, and King David also rejoiced greatly. They gave with joy, not with sorrow (wrong_detail). The text emphasizes unanimity — there was no quarreling over who gave more (wrong_detail). Tax exemption is never mentioned anywhere in this passage (wrong_scope).

content: In his prayer, what image did David use to describe the human condition before God, and what did that image emphasize?
options: Like strangers and sojourners, whose days pass like a shadow with no lasting hope
Like faithful servants entrusted by their master to manage an inheritance for a long time
Like heirs who firmly possess the promised land forever
Like soldiers who guard the city walls day and night until their last breath
explanation: 1 Chronicles 29:15 says: 'we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were. Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding.' The image emphasizes the transience and fragility of human life. 'Faithful servants entrusted with long-term management' echoes the spirit of stewardship but contradicts the meaning of 'sojourners, like a shadow' in this verse (wrong_detail). 'Heirs who firmly possess the land forever' inverts the humble acknowledgment of human frailty (common_misconception). 'Soldiers guarding the city' is simply not the image the text uses (wrong_scope).

content: Solomon was crowned king a second time, and at the same time another person was anointed as priest. Who was that person?
options: Zadok
Abiathar
Eleazar
Jehoiada
explanation: 1 Chronicles 29:22 records that they made Solomon king and anointed him, and also anointed Zadok as priest. Abiathar was a priest of the same era but had been deposed — he is not the one anointed here (near_passage). Eleazar was Aaron's son in the time of Moses, from a different period altogether (wrong_scope). Jehoiada was a prominent priest in the time of Joash, much later, and has no connection to this event (wrong_detail).

content: The text summarizes David's life at the time of his death with what characteristics, showing how complete his life had been?
options: Old age, full of days, riches, and honor
Poor but full of faith and peace
Died in battle while defending Jerusalem
Tormented by illness throughout his final years
explanation: 1 Chronicles 29:28 records that David died 'in a good old age, full of days, riches, and honor.' His life is described as full and complete, not poor — though he was indeed a man of deep faith (true_but_off). David did not die in battle; he passed away in old age (wrong_detail). The text says nothing about him being tormented by illness in his final years — that detail is fabricated and contradicts the text (wrong_detail).

content: At the close of the book, in whose records — seers and prophets — are the deeds of King David said to be written?
options: Samuel, Nathan, and Gad
Elijah, Elisha, and Micah
Moses, Aaron, and Joshua
Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel
explanation: 1 Chronicles 29:29 records that the deeds of King David were written in the records of Samuel the seer, the records of Nathan the prophet, and the records of Gad the seer. Elijah, Elisha, and Micah were prophets of a later era and have no connection to David's life (wrong_scope). Moses, Aaron, and Joshua belonged to the time of the Exodus — a completely different period (wrong_scope). Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel were major later prophets who did not record the history of David here (wrong_detail).
